notes.h: Scale and pace of urban growth
points: Most of the world's urban growth now takes place in developing countries in Asia, Africa and Latin America.
About 30% of the world's population was urban in 1950 and about 55% in 2018 (UN, World Urbanization Prospects 2018).
Over half of the world's population has been urban since about 2007.
The UN projects that about 68% of the world's population will be urban by 2050.
Close to 90% of the increase to 2050 is expected in Asia and Africa; India, China and Nigeria together account for over a third of it.
Megacities, with over 10 million people, are a growing feature of urbanisation in the developing world.
UN-Habitat estimates that over 1 billion people live in slums or informal settlements.

notes.b: Cities grow through natural increase and through migration. The migration theory itself is covered in the note Rural-to-urban migration in developed and developing regions.
points: Natural increase: the urban population is young, birth rates are high and death rates have fallen.
Push factors: rural poverty, landlessness, small farms, mechanisation, drought and crop failure, lack of services, conflict and natural disasters.
Pull factors: jobs in the formal and informal sectors, higher wages, schools and hospitals, perceived opportunities, and family already living in the city.
Primate cities attract investment and government spending, which reinforces their pull on migrants.
Migrants with little money and no legal land settle in shanty towns, slums and informal settlements, called bustees, favelas, chawls or jhopadpattis depending on the country.
These settlements are built on marginal land: river banks, steep slopes, beside railways, rubbish dumps and floodplains.
Tenure is insecure, so residents can be evicted and have no legal right to the land they occupy.
Overcrowding is severe, and some people have no shelter at all, living as homeless pavement dwellers.
Without piped water or sewers, settlements rely on open drains and shared toilets.
Contaminated water and waste spread water-borne disease: cholera, typhoid and dysentery.
Many residents work in the informal sector as street vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste pickers and home workers.
Informal work offers no job security and low pay; child labour is part of informal employment.
Underemployment means that people have work but not enough of it to earn a living.
Road networks cannot cope with the growth in traffic, so journeys take longer and congestion becomes permanent.
Trains and buses are overcrowded at peak times.
Road deaths are a serious problem in the city.
Air pollution comes from traffic, industry and cooking fuels burned in crowded homes.
Untreated sewage and industrial waste are discharged into rivers.
Rubbish is not collected in many areas, so it builds up in streets and drains.
Monsoon or tropical downpours flood low-lying, paved and badly drained land, where settlements are often built.
Hillside slums are at risk of landslides, and crowded, poorly built homes are at risk of fire.
Crime and drugs are social problems, and street children live and work on the streets.
Rich and poor districts sit side by side, so inequality is visible within the city.
Local government is weak, so it struggles to provide services.
Slum clearance removes informal settlements by demolition and eviction.
It usually fails, because residents are moved further out or into new slums and the underlying problems remain.
The authorities provide serviced plots with water, drains and power.
Residents build their own homes on these plots, which is known as aided self-help.
Lanes are paved, water taps, toilets, drains and electricity are installed, and residents are given secure tenure.
Because the community stays in place, people can improve their own homes over time.
Planned satellite towns and new towns divert growth away from the overcrowded core.
Examples are given in the Mumbai case study (Navi Mumbai) and the Kolkata case study (Salt Lake and New Town).
Metros, suburban rail and bus rapid transit move large numbers of people without adding more cars to the roads.
Curitiba in Brazil is the leading example of bus rapid transit, described below.

notes.h: Solution example: Curitiba, Brazil (bus rapid transit)
points: Bus rapid transit began in Curitiba in 1974 under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner.
Dedicated bus lanes and raised tube stations allow fast boarding, which reduces car use.
Recyclable waste could be exchanged for food or bus tokens.
The model has been copied worldwide, for example in Bogotá's TransMilenio (2000).
Rural development, land reform and jobs in smaller cities give people reasons to stay in rural areas.
NGOs and community groups also act on these problems, as the Missionaries of Charity do in Kolkata.
Kolkata lies on the Hooghly river near the Bay of Bengal, on low-lying delta land.
It was founded in 1690 by the British East India Company (Job Charnock).
It developed as a port on the Hooghly, with jute mills; Howrah Bridge across the river opened in 1943.
It was the capital of British India until 1911.
The city was renamed from Calcutta to Kolkata in 2001.
It was a colonial port and administrative capital, and its jute and engineering industries attracted migrants from Bihar, Odisha and rural Bengal.
The Bengal famine of 1943 drove millions of rural people towards the city.
Partition in 1947 brought refugees, and the 1971 Bangladesh Liberation War brought a further wave.
Natural increase adds to the population, and the city has regional primacy in eastern India.
Census 2011 gave an urban agglomeration of about 14.1 million people.
Bustees (slums) house many of the city's poorest people, in overcrowded conditions.
Pavement dwellers have no shelter and live on the streets.
Census 2011 counted about 65 million people in slums across India; this is an India-wide figure.
Partition cut the city off from the jute-growing lands that became East Pakistan, so the economy declined.
Jobs did not keep pace with migrants, so many people depend on informal work.
Informal work includes hand-pulled rickshaws; Kolkata is one of the few cities in the world where these still operate.

notes.h: Kolkata: water, flooding, pollution and traffic
points: Water supply and sewerage are poor, so many residents lack safe water and proper sanitation.
Monsoon rain floods the low-lying streets of the city.
Air pollution and traffic congestion add to the city's environmental problems.
The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, the city's planning body, was set up in 1970.
From the 1970s its bustee improvement programme provided water taps, toilets, paved lanes and drains.
Kolkata Metro, India's first, opened in 1984.
Salt Lake City (Bidhannagar) is a planned township built from the 1960s on reclaimed wetland east of the city; its Sector V is an IT hub.
New Town (Rajarhat) was planned from the late 1990s, with IT parks.
The East Kolkata Wetlands were designated a Ramsar wetland of international importance in 2002; their fish ponds and fields use and naturally treat much of the city's sewage.
Mother Teresa founded the Missionaries of Charity in the city in 1950 and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
Bustee upgrading improved conditions for many residents, but slums remain.
The new towns serve the middle classes more than the poor.
Mumbai was originally seven islands, joined together by land reclamation, with a deep, sheltered natural harbour.
It was a British East India Company port, and cotton mills were built there from the 19th century.
Mumbai is India's financial capital, not its political capital; it houses the Reserve Bank of India headquarters and the Bombay Stock Exchange, founded in 1875, Asia's oldest.
It is the centre of the Bollywood film industry.
The city was renamed from Bombay in 1995.
Migrants come from across India, including Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, drawn by industry and jobs.
Census 2011 gave a Greater Mumbai urban agglomeration of about 18.4 million people.
Dharavi is one of Asia's largest slums, in central Mumbai, with many small home-based industries such as recycling, leather and pottery.
Land and housing costs are very high on the narrow peninsula, which limits the space available for housing.

notes.h: Mumbai: transport, flooding and water problems
points: The suburban railway carries several million passengers a day, and its trains are overcrowded.
Road congestion adds to the pressure on the transport network.
On 26 July 2005 about 944 mm of rain fell in one day at Santacruz, flooding the city.
Water supply and sanitation cannot keep pace with the dense population.
The Great Bombay textile strike of 1982 led to the closure of most cotton mills.
Mill land was later redeveloped, so the city's industrial base changed.

notes.h: Mumbai: planned growth at Navi Mumbai
points: Navi Mumbai is a planned twin city across the harbour, begun in the 1970s by CIDCO (City and Industrial Development Corporation of Maharashtra, set up 1970).
It is designed to take population and industry away from the crowded core of Mumbai.
The Slum Rehabilitation Authority, set up in 1995, lets developers rehouse slum dwellers free in new blocks and sell the remaining flats.
The Dharavi Redevelopment Project was awarded to the Adani Group in 2022.
Mumbai Metro Line 1 opened in 2014.
The Bandra–Worli Sea Link opened in 2009.
The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), opened in January 2024, is India's longest sea bridge and links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai.
Rehousing flats under the Slum Rehabilitation Authority are criticised for poor design.
Rehousing is also criticised for breaking up Dharavi's home-based industries.

notes.h: São Paulo, Brazil: site and early history
points: São Paulo lies on a plateau inland from the port of Santos, not on the coast.
It was founded on 25 January 1554 by Jesuit missionaries.
Santos is now Latin America's busiest container port.
Coffee wealth in the 19th century was exported through Santos and carried by the Santos–Jundiaí railway, opened in 1867.
Immigration from Europe, especially Italy, in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.
Japanese immigration began in 1908 with the ship Kasato Maru; the city has the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centred on the Liberdade district.
From the 1950s São Paulo became Brazil's industrial heartland; car plants, including Volkswagen, opened in the ABC region (Santo André, São Bernardo do Campo and São Caetano do Sul).
Migrants from the drought-prone North-East of Brazil, known as nordestinos, moved to the city to work in its industries.
IBGE Census 2022 gave the city of São Paulo about 11.5 million people and the metropolitan region about 21 million.
São Paulo is the largest city in South America and in the Southern Hemisphere.
Brazil is over 80% urban.
Paraisópolis favela borders the wealthy district of Morumbi, so extreme inequality is visible from one street to the next.
Heliópolis is São Paulo's largest favela.
Crime is a problem in the city, including in its favelas.

notes.h: São Paulo: traffic, pollution and flooding
points: Traffic congestion is severe across the metropolitan region.
Air pollution from vehicles and industry adds to the city's environmental problems.
The Tietê river flows through the city and floods in heavy summer rain.
The Cantareira reservoir system is the main source of the city's water.
During the 2014–2015 drought the Cantareira fell to very low levels, and water rationing was introduced.
Rodízio, from 1997: cars are banned from central São Paulo at rush hours on one weekday, according to the last digit of the number plate.
The São Paulo Metro opened its first line in 1974.
The Rodoanel Mário Covas ring road encircles the metropolitan region; its first section opened in 2002.
Projeto Cingapura (1990s) replaced some favela shacks with apartment blocks on the same sites.
Minha Casa, Minha Vida, a national subsidised housing programme, was launched in 2009.
Favela upgrading and transport improvements have helped.
Favelas and traffic congestion persist.

keyTerms.definition: A city with over 10 million people.
Growth of a population through births exceeding deaths, without migration.
A condition in rural areas, such as poverty or drought, that drives people to leave.
A feature of a city, such as jobs or services, that attracts migrants.
The largest city in a country, which is much bigger than any other and dominates its economy.
Unregulated work with no job security, such as street vending or waste picking.
An Indian term for a slum or informal settlement.
A Brazilian term for a slum or informal settlement built on land occupied without legal title.
A scheme in which the authorities provide serviced plots and residents build their own homes.
Improving an existing settlement in place with services, paving and secure tenure.
The São Paulo scheme banning cars from central streets at rush hours by number-plate digit.

factCards.term: World urbanisation: UN figures for 1950, 2018 and 2050
factCards.definition: About 30% of the world's population was urban in 1950 and about 55% in 2018, projected about 68% by 2050; over half urban since about 2007. Close to 90% of the increase to 2050 is expected in Asia and Africa. Over 1 billion people live in slums (UN-Habitat).

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: reasons for rapid growth
factCards.definition: Natural increase: a young population, high birth rates, falling death rates. Push: rural poverty, landlessness, mechanisation, drought, conflict. Pull: jobs, higher wages, schools, hospitals, family in the city. Primate cities draw investment.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: housing problems
factCards.definition: Slums on marginal land: river banks, steep slopes, beside railways, rubbish dumps and floodplains; insecure tenure, so residents can be evicted; severe overcrowding; homeless pavement dwellers.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: health, employment and transport problems
factCards.definition: No piped water or sewers, so open drains spread cholera, typhoid and dysentery; informal work (vendors, rickshaw pullers, waste pickers) with low pay, no security, child labour and underemployment; overcrowded trains and buses; congestion; road deaths.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: pollution, hazards and social problems
factCards.definition: Air pollution from traffic, industry and cooking fuels; untreated sewage in rivers; uncollected rubbish; floods on low, badly drained land, landslides on hillside slums, fires; crime, drugs, street children, visible inequality, weak local government.

factCards.term: Slum solutions: why clearance fails and what works better
factCards.definition: Clearance by demolition and eviction usually fails, moving people further out or into new slums. Site-and-service schemes and upgrading in place (paving, taps, toilets, drains, power, secure tenure) keep people housed and let them improve their own homes.

factCards.term: Developing-world cities: other solutions with named examples
factCards.definition: Satellite and new towns divert growth (Navi Mumbai; Kolkata's Salt Lake and New Town); metros, suburban rail and bus rapid transit (Curitiba); rural development, land reform and jobs in smaller cities slow migration; NGOs and community groups help.

factCards.term: Curitiba: how its bus rapid transit works and who copied it
factCards.definition: Begun in 1974 under architect-mayor Jaime Lerner with dedicated bus lanes; raised tube stations for fast boarding were added later; the system cut car use and was copied by Bogotá's TransMilenio (2000). Recyclable waste could be exchanged for food or bus tokens.

factCards.term: Kolkata: site and history with dates
factCards.definition: On the Hooghly near the Bay of Bengal, on low-lying delta land; founded in 1690 by the British East India Company (Job Charnock); capital of British India until 1911; a port with jute mills; Howrah Bridge opened 1943; renamed from Calcutta in 2001.

factCards.term: Kolkata: reasons for growth
factCards.definition: Colonial port and capital; jute and engineering jobs drew migrants from Bihar, Odisha and rural Bengal; the 1943 Bengal famine; refugees after Partition (1947) and the 1971 Bangladesh war; natural increase. About 14.1 million in Census 2011.

factCards.term: Kolkata: problems of rapid growth
factCards.definition: Bustees and pavement dwellers; overcrowding; poor water and sewerage; monsoon flooding of low-lying streets; air pollution and congestion; Partition cut off the jute lands, so jobs lagged and many rely on informal work, including hand-pulled rickshaws.

factCards.definition: Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority, 1970: bustee improvement with taps, toilets, paved lanes and drains; India's first metro, 1984; Salt Lake City (Bidhannagar) from the 1960s, with the Sector V IT hub; New Town (Rajarhat) from the late 1990s.

factCards.definition: East Kolkata Wetlands, a Ramsar site since 2002, naturally treat much of the city's sewage; Mother Teresa's Missionaries of Charity (1950; Nobel Peace Prize 1979). Upgrading improved conditions, but slums remain and the new towns serve the middle classes.

factCards.definition: Favelas: Paraisópolis beside wealthy Morumbi, and Heliópolis, the largest; extreme inequality; severe congestion and air pollution; the Tietê floods in summer rain; the 2014–2015 drought drained the Cantareira reservoirs, causing rationing; crime.

questions.prompt: Discuss the problems that can arise from the growth of cities in the developing world.
questions.model: Housing is the first problem. Rapid migration has produced bustees, which are overcrowded slums, and pavement dwellers who have no shelter, as in Kolkata. Settlements are built on marginal and low-lying land, so housing is insecure. Water and sewerage are poor, so disease spreads and people lack safe water. Monsoon rain floods the low-lying streets of Kolkata, and flooding damages homes that are already poorly built. Air pollution and traffic congestion add to the city's environmental problems. Employment is a problem because jobs did not keep pace with migrants after Partition cut Kolkata off from its jute hinterland, so many people depend on informal work such as hand-pulled rickshaws. Informal work has no job security and low pay. Social problems include crime and inequality between rich and poor districts. The Census 2011 urban agglomeration of about 14.1 million people shows that the problems affect a very large population. Overall, the growth of the city has outpaced the provision of housing, services and jobs.

questions.prompt: (i) Name one developing-world city that is growing rapidly. (ii) Explain the reasons for its growth. (iii) Describe the problems caused. (iv) Explain one solution.
questions.model: (i) São Paulo, Brazil, is growing rapidly and is the largest city in South America. (ii) Its growth began with coffee wealth in the 19th century, exported through the port of Santos and carried by the Santos–Jundiaí railway from 1867. European immigration, and Japanese immigration from 1908, added to the population. From the 1950s the city became Brazil's industrial heartland, and car plants in the ABC region drew migrants. Migrants from the drought-prone North-East came to work in industry, and the city grew to about 11.5 million people in the city of São Paulo by 2022. (iii) Favelas such as Heliópolis, São Paulo's largest, house many poor people, and Paraisópolis lies beside the wealthy district of Morumbi, which shows extreme inequality. Traffic congestion and air pollution are serious. The Tietê river floods in heavy summer rain. The 2014–2015 drought reduced the Cantareira reservoir system to very low levels, and water rationing followed. Crime is a major problem. (iv) The rodízio scheme, introduced in 1997, bans cars from central São Paulo at rush hours on one weekday, according to the last digit of the number plate. Drivers must use other transport on their banned day, and the metro, whose first line opened in 1974, is one alternative. Favela upgrading and the Projeto Cingapura flats, which replaced some shacks with apartment blocks, are further responses. The rodízio has been a response to traffic congestion, but congestion persists.

questions.prompt: Examine the measures taken to solve the problems of one developing-world city.
questions.model: Mumbai has used several measures. Navi Mumbai, a planned twin city across the harbour begun in the 1970s by CIDCO, set up in 1970, was designed to take population and industry away from the crowded core. It is a long-term planned response, so it does not directly improve the slums that already exist. The Slum Rehabilitation Authority, set up in 1995, lets developers rehouse slum dwellers free in new blocks and sell the remaining flats. This tackles housing directly, but rehousing flats are criticised for poor design and for breaking up Dharavi's home-based industries. The Dharavi Redevelopment Project, awarded to the Adani Group in 2022, applies the same approach to Dharavi, one of Asia's largest slums. Transport measures include Mumbai Metro Line 1, opened in 2014, and the Bandra–Worli Sea Link, opened in 2009. The Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Setu), opened in January 2024, links Mumbai to Navi Mumbai and is India's longest sea bridge. Transport measures address congestion and the overcrowded suburban railway, but they do not directly improve housing for slum dwellers. Overall, the measures tackle different problems, and the housing schemes are the most criticised.
